sections.title: FOREFRONT - Rent Board & Rent Increase License: individual owner

rows.label: Does an individual (non-corporate) owner still need the license?
rows.value: Yes - SF.gov states 'a landlord must get a rent increase license before imposing annual allowable and/or banked rent increases'; no individual-owner exception is stated on the official pages re-fetched 2026-11-07
rows.notes: Ownership form (individual vs corporation) is not listed as an exemption. Do not rely on being a small/individual owner.

rows.label: Small buildings (1-9 units) timing
rows.value: Requirement effective July 1, 2022; March 1, 2023 for condominiums and buildings with 1-9 residential units
rows.notes: A small individual-owned building is therefore covered now (2026).

rows.label: Step 1 - Report to the Rent Board (Housing Inventory)
rows.value: All owners of residential property are required to report through the Rent Board Portal; reporting is free, online 24/7, due March 1 every year
rows.notes: This reporting is how you 'inform the Rent Board'. Information submitted is public; submit under penalty of perjury.

rows.label: Step 2 - License is generated
rows.value: Property owners who report a unit as tenant-occupied receive a rent increase license; it is automatically generated for non-owner-occupied units
rows.notes: The license does not need to be included with the rent increase notice to tenants.

rows.label: Step 3 - License must be current BEFORE the effective date
rows.value: A current Rent Increase License must be on file before an annual or banked increase takes effect. Safest sequence: report, verify license, then serve notice.
rows.notes: Official pages state the effective-date condition; they do not expressly require a separate Board filing before mailing an ordinary annual/banked notice. See F25.

rows.label: Late reporting
rows.value: You can still submit and receive a license after the March 1 deadline; the Rent Board does not assess monetary penalties for late filing - but the increase notice is not enforceable without a license on the effective date
rows.notes: Late filing has no monetary penalty, but do not assume it retroactively cures an already-served notice; get legal advice on any prior notice.

rows.label: Step 4 - Serve a compliant tenant notice
rows.value: 30-day written notice (90-day if >10% alone/combined in same year; +5 days if mailed) stating dollar amount, percentage and effective date, using the rate in effect on the increase date
rows.notes: Check lease type, anniversary, retaliation and notice law; license alone is not enough.

rows.label: Can tenants check?
rows.value: Tenants can search the Rent Board Portal to see if their landlord is up to date with their rent increase license; if you miss the deadline the Rent Board may notify tenants you are not in compliance
rows.notes: Assume tenants and free tenant-side legal services can and will check this before paying an increase.

process.title: Step-by-Step: Rent Board License and Notice
process.description: The direct answer to the licensing question, the ordinance text, the 12-step process, and how it applies to the two anonymized units.

rows.label: Must an individual property owner (not a corporation) get a Rent Increase License before raising rent?
rows.value: Yes. A landlord must have a current Rent Increase License on file before any annual or banked increase can take effect. The requirement follows the unit's rent-controlled status, not the owner's size or corporate form.
rows.notes: No owner-type, individual-owner or small-portfolio exemption appears on the official pages.

rows.label: What does the Rent Ordinance itself say?
rows.value: Section 37.3(a)(1): a landlord who has reported the required information under Section 37.15 shall have a license to impose an annual increase not exceeding 60% of the published CPI increase, never more than 7%. Section 37.15(e): a substantially compliant owner receives the license; otherwise it is suspended and the tenant is not obligated to pay the increased rent for the months of the suspension.
rows.notes: The license condition is written into the ordinance, not only the SF.gov summaries.

rows.label: Is there a small-owner or fewer-than-10-unit exemption?
rows.value: No exemption found. Condominiums and units in buildings with fewer than 10 residential units have been required to report since March 1, 2023, with updates every March 1.
rows.notes: Applies to this two-unit building if the units are rent-controlled.

rows.label: Must the owner report into the Housing Inventory first?
rows.value: Yes. All owners of residential property are required to report; a rent increase license is generated for units reported as tenant-occupied.
rows.notes: Free; annual deadline March 1; no monetary penalty for late filing.

rows.label: Does informing the Rent Board mean filing each increase notice?
rows.value: The official pages describe the license as arising from the annual Housing Inventory report. No separate filing of an individual increase notice is described, and the license does not need to be included with the notice.
rows.notes: Absence of a stated separate filing requirement is not an official confirmation; ordinary annual/banked increases differ from petition-based increases.

rows.label: What happens if a notice goes into effect without a current license?
rows.value: The notice may be null and void (possibly for multiple years) or unenforceable, depending on the SF.gov page; the tenant may be entitled to a refund and may file a Tenant Petition for Unlawful Rent Increase for an Administrative Law Judge hearing.
rows.notes: Wording differs between SF.gov pages - see flag F25.

rows.label: Does the license requirement cover every kind of increase?
rows.value: It covers annual allowable and banked increases on rent-controlled units. SF.gov states it is not required for Section 6.14/Costa-Hawkins increases or for passthroughs allowed under the Rent Ordinance.
rows.notes: Those increases have their own notice and petition rules.

rows.label: Is the Housing Inventory information public?
rows.value: Yes. SF.gov states the information entered in the Housing Inventory submission is public, and may include name and business, contact information, approximate square footage, bedrooms, bathrooms and vacancy/occupancy history.
rows.notes: Privacy note: the required filing publishes the owner's name and business contact information.

rows.label: Does the license requirement apply if the unit is not rent-controlled?
rows.value: No. SF.gov states the Rent Increase License rules apply only to units under San Francisco rent control.
rows.notes: Coverage of the specific address is unverified in this case.

rows.label: Step 1 - Confirm the unit is under the Rent Ordinance
rows.value: Many units built on or before June 13, 1979 that are not single-family dwellings have rent control; check the address in the SF Planning Property Information Map. Partial exemptions exist.
rows.notes: Exact address not supplied in this case.

rows.label: Step 2 - Create a Rent Board Portal account
rows.value: Owners create an account in the Rent Board Portal to reach the Housing Inventory and the license record; paper filings can be emailed to the Rent Board or dropped off at its office.
rows.notes: Office open 9-4 weekdays; counseling 415-252-4600.

rows.label: Step 3 - Report each unit into the Housing Inventory
rows.value: Report by March 1 each year (buildings under 10 units since March 1, 2023) under penalty of perjury: owner or manager contact, square footage, bedrooms, bathrooms, occupancy date and base rent in $250 increments.
rows.notes: Reporting is free; no monetary penalty is assessed for late filing.

rows.label: Step 4 - Confirm a current license for each unit
rows.value: The license is generated for tenant-occupied units after reporting and must be current on the effective date of the increase, not merely later.
rows.notes: Check status by address or APN in the portal.

rows.label: Step 5 - Fix the anniversary date
rows.value: For an eligible periodic tenancy, the first annual increase may take effect 12 months after the tenancy began; after an increase, the increase date becomes the anniversary date.
rows.notes: Fixed-term leases need an express increase clause; actual lease type is unverified (F36).

rows.label: Step 6 - Use the rate in effect on the effective date
rows.value: 1.6% for increases effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027; the rate is 60% of the Bay Area CPI-U increase and Section 37.3 caps it at 7%.
rows.notes: No rate published yet for increases on or after 3/1/27 - flag F27.

rows.label: Step 7 - Decide whether a banked increase applies
rows.value: A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase; banked percentages are added together, never compounded or prorated, never carry to a new tenant, and need no Rent Board petition.
rows.notes: SF.gov text/examples conflict on 12 vs 24 months; verify history and obtain counselor/legal review before relying on banking (F03).

rows.label: Step 8 - Calculate on base rent only and do not round up
rows.value: Multiply base rent (including parking or storage charges) by the total percentage; temporary passthroughs and fluctuating charges are excluded, and the result is not rounded up.
rows.notes: See the Calculations page for the illustrative arithmetic.

rows.label: Step 9 - File any petition or worksheet before the notice
rows.value: File required petitions before notice; file utility worksheets before notice; bond/water passthroughs use their specific worksheet rules.
rows.notes: A plain annual or banked increase needs no petition. Do not treat every passthrough as petition-based.

rows.label: Step 10 - Serve written notice with the required contents
rows.value: At least 30 days' written notice, or 90 days if the increase by itself or combined with another increase in the same year is more than 10%; add 5 days if mailed. State the dollar amount, the percentage, the effective date and any banked portion.
rows.notes: Civil Code 827 requires longer notice in some cases.

rows.label: Step 11 - Deliver it properly and keep proof
rows.value: Personal delivery or mail under Civil Code 827 and Code of Civil Procedure 1013; keep the notice, proof of service and the license record with the unit file.
rows.notes: The license need not be attached to the notice.

rows.label: Step 12 - Expect tenant-side review and apply the same rule to each unit
rows.value: Tenant petitions are free and have no filing deadline for an unlawful increase; a tenant may search the portal for license status. Apply the same written, neutral, dated process to every eligible unit.
rows.notes: No rule requires raising both units - see Analysis.

fee.title: Rent Board Fee & Other Registrations
fee.description: The second, separate Rent Board obligation: the annual per-unit fee, its March 1 deadline, penalties, exemptions, the 50% tenant recovery, and City business registration.

sections.title: Fee basics - a separate obligation from the Rent Increase License

rows.label: Who must pay the Rent Board Fee
rows.value: An owner of a residential dwelling unit or guest unit must pay a Rent Board Fee each year unless there is a current exemption on file with the Rent Board or a Homeowners' Exemption on file with the Assessor-Recorder. No individual-owner or small-building exception is stated.
rows.notes: This is a fee obligation, not a licence application.

rows.label: What the fee is charged on
rows.value: All residential property owners must pay a per-unit fee unless the unit has a current exemption. This includes single-family homes and condominiums, units built after 1979, vacant units, and units occupied by friends or family members.
rows.notes: Rent-control coverage is not the test for the fee; exemption is.

rows.label: Amount for the 2026-2027 tax year
rows.value: $59.00 per dwelling unit; $29.50 per guest unit (single room occupancy or SRO/residential hotel room). The 50% tenant share is $29.50 per dwelling unit or $14.75 per guest unit.
rows.notes: Form 573 confirms $59.00 per unit for 7/21-6/22 through 7/25-6/26 (flag F40 on the form's title metadata).

rows.label: Paying the fee does not make you licensed
rows.value: SF.gov states that requesting a Rent Board Fee exemption does not satisfy Housing Inventory reporting requirements, and the 2027 informational notice states the reverse: Housing Inventory reporting does not satisfy a fee exemption. The licence arises only from the Housing Inventory report.
rows.notes: Two separate obligations; no official page found conditions the licence on fee payment (flag F41).

rows.label: How and where to pay
rows.value: Preferred: credit card or electronic check (ACH) online through the Rent Board Portal. In person: Office of the Treasurer and Tax Collector, City Hall Room 140. By mail: San Francisco Rent Board, PO Box 7429, San Francisco, CA 94120-7429. No payments are accepted at the Rent Board office.
rows.notes: A dishonoured check or eCheck adds a $50.00 payment failure fee.

rows.label: Statutory scope of Chapter 37A
rows.value: Chapter 37A applies to all residential units in San Francisco, including units exempt from the Chapter 37 rent-increase limitations under the Costa-Hawkins Act or Section 37.3(d), with listed exclusions (nonprofit co-ops, licensed care facilities and dormitories, government-regulated rents such as Section 8, tourist-use guest rooms, and units with a current homeowners' exemption).
rows.notes: Ordinance text, not just the SF.gov summary.

sections.title: Deadlines, penalties and the 2026-27 compliance calendar

rows.label: Due date and late penalties
rows.value: The fee is due March 1 each year. A 5% late penalty is added if unpaid by March 1, a further 5% if unpaid by April 1, and a further 5% if unpaid by May 1 - a maximum penalty of 15%.
rows.notes: SF.gov and Section 37A.4 agree on the March/April/May sequence.

rows.label: Delinquency and referral to the Bureau of Delinquent Revenue
rows.value: SF.gov states that fees not paid in full by June 1 will be referred to the Bureau of Delinquent Revenue with additional costs added to the principal charges; its timeline instead says a Notice of Delinquent Payment is mailed in July, after which the owner has 30 days before referral. Section 37A.4 says the matter is referred if the fee remains outstanding as of June 1.
rows.notes: The official page is internally inconsistent - see flag F38. Manual confirmation with 311 is advised.

rows.label: Payment failure fee
rows.value: If a check or eCheck payment is not honoured by the bank, the payment is null and void and a $50.00 payment failure fee is charged in addition to any late payment penalties.
rows.notes: Not recoverable from a tenant.

rows.label: Exemption request window and annual refiling
rows.value: Requests for exemption are submitted through the Rent Board Portal between October and early December, and an exemption request must be submitted every year. For the 2027 fee the deadline is Monday, December 14, 2026; units without a valid approved exemption are billed for the fee due March 1, 2027.
rows.notes: Homeowners' Exemption holders do not refile yearly with the Rent Board.

rows.label: 2026-27 calendar as published
rows.value: October: informational notices mailed, exemption window opens. December 14, 2026: exemption request deadline. January 2027: annual notices (fee invoices) mailed. March 1, 2027: fee due with no penalty; first 5% penalty from March 2. April 1 and May 1: second and third 5% penalties. May 31, 11:59 pm: last day to pay with all penalties. June 1: outstanding bills delinquent. July: notice of delinquent payment mailed.
rows.notes: Housing Inventory reporting is also due March 1, 2027 - see the Step-by-Step License page.

sections.title: Exemptions are narrow - a rented unit is not exempt

rows.label: Owner-occupied exemption
rows.value: A single-family home, condominium, co-op or apartment unit occupied by an owner of record and not rented at any time may qualify. Vacant units, and units occupied solely by children or close relatives who are not on title as owner, do not qualify. Section 37A.1(f) requires the owner to file an affidavit with the Rent Board.
rows.notes: Both units here are rented, so this exemption would not apply on the owner-supplied facts.

rows.label: Other exemption categories
rows.value: Government-controlled or regulated rents (for example Section 8, with documentation), hotel guest rooms designed for tourist use under the Residential Hotel Ordinance, housing in hospitals, monasteries, extended-care facilities and licensed homes for the elderly, dormitories owned by educational institutions, and nonprofit cooperatives owned, occupied and controlled by a majority of residents.
rows.notes: Documentation is required for each category.

rows.label: Homeowners' Exemption route
rows.value: An owner whose unit is the primary residence and who already has a Homeowners' Exemption through the Assessor-Recorder should not be assessed the Rent Board fee and may email proof to the Rent Board. The Homeowners' Exemption applies only to the current fee cycle and cannot be applied retroactively unless it appeared on earlier property tax statements.
rows.notes: The Rent Board does not process Homeowners' Exemption applications.

sections.title: Recovering 50% of the fee from tenants - not a rent increase

rows.label: Maximum recovery and who can be charged
rows.value: An owner who has paid the fee in full may recover up to 50% of the annual fee (exclusive of any penalties) from the tenant(s) in occupancy of each unit on November 1 of the applicable tax year. For 2026-2027 that is $29.50 per dwelling unit.
rows.notes: Only tenants in occupancy on or before November 1 can be billed.

rows.label: How the recovery may be made
rows.value: By deducting the amount from the next security-deposit interest payment owed to the tenant, or by billing the tenant directly - but direct billing is allowed only where there is no or insufficient security deposit held, or where the owner already pays the deposit interest annually. The bill must state the amount for that unit, that the purpose is to fund the Rent Board and related administrative costs, and that the amount is due and payable within 30 days of the bill.
rows.notes: Do not net it into the rent figure on a rent-increase notice.

rows.label: Banking an unrecovered fee
rows.value: A fee not recovered in the year the owner was first entitled to it may be banked and collected from that tenant in a future year. Only fees that became due after July 25, 1999 may be banked, and the billing statement must show the fee owed for each year and any interest due for each year.
rows.notes: Banking is by deposit-interest deduction except where no or insufficient interest exists.

rows.label: If the tenant does not pay
rows.value: A tenant's failure to pay the Rent Board fee is not a just cause for eviction; the landlord must go to Small Claims Court to collect an unpaid fee.
rows.notes: The owner remains liable to the Rent Board either way (Section 37A.6(d)).

rows.label: Security-deposit interest rate used for a deduction
rows.value: The interest rate owed on deposits for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 4.2%. Interest is paid annually on the tenant's annual due date for deposits held over one year and may not be compounded. AB 12 caps a deposit at one month's rent (two months for a qualifying small natural-person owner), for deposits collected on or after July 1, 2024.
rows.notes: This is the amount a fee recovery is deducted from.

rows.label: How a 50% recovery is divided among several co-tenants
rows.notes: No official page states how the 50% is allocated among multiple co-tenants of one unit. Left blank rather than inferred (flag F42).

rows.label: Recovery is not part of the rent increase
rows.value: The fee recovery is a separate statutory billing mechanism tied to the security-deposit interest cycle; it is not an annual or banked rent increase, does not change the base rent, and is not covered by the Rent Increase License precondition for annual/banked increases.
rows.notes: Keep the two documents and the two amounts visibly separate.

sections.title: Other registration question - City business registration

rows.label: Does an individual small owner need a City business registration certificate?
rows.value: A person receiving rental income from one residential structure consisting of fewer than four units, or from one residential condominium, is not - by reason of that fact alone - required to obtain a business registration certificate. Other business activity or payroll expense may require one. A lessor is treated as a separate person for each individual building, the Tax Collector decides what a separate building is and how many units it has, and a return must be filed unless the lessor leases fewer than 4 units in any individual building.
rows.notes: Rule only. For this owner it depends on facts not supplied - see the next row.

rows.label: What the Housing Inventory asks for
rows.value: Section 37.15(b)(2)(B) requires the business registration number for the unit, if any - so reporting does not assume that every owner has one.
rows.notes: Absence of a business registration number is not, by itself, a reporting failure.

questions.title: All User Questions Answered
questions.description: Direct answers with official source links; blanks where official confirmation is absent.

rows.label: What are reasonable/normal rental increases under local, state and federal law?
rows.value: Local 1.6% for covered units; state-only AB 1482 8.8% does not replace SF limits; no official general federal private-rent cap found. HUD FMR is not a cap.
rows.notes: Federal cap blank and flagged.

rows.label: How do big real estate corporations handle increases?
rows.value: Public REITs disclose lease-over-lease rates in SEC filings: IRT Q4 2025 renewal 2.9%, new -3.7%, blended 0.8%; Invitation Homes 2025 renewal 4.6%, new -0.8%.
rows.notes: Portfolio-level, not SF-specific; no generalization.

rows.label: How do individual SF property owners handle increases?
rows.value: Official rules require the annual allowable increase, license, 12-month timing and notice; June 2024 Rent Board workload shows 23 landlord petitions/154 units.
rows.notes: Narrow formal-petition evidence only.

rows.label: What is the correct tenant-notice method?
rows.value: Written 30-day notice; 90-day if >10% alone/combined in same year; +5 days if mailed; dollar amount, percentage, effective date; banked portion if any; license first; 827 delivery rules.
rows.notes: Conservative checklist capable of lawyer review.

rows.label: What are reasonable reasons for increases?
rows.value: Annual CPI-based allowable increase, properly banked skipped/partial increases, and Rent Board-approved petition/worksheet passthroughs; not extra rent merely because a roommate moved in.
rows.notes: Mere long tenure below market is not extraordinary.

rows.label: What tenant-friendly advocate/lawyer scrutiny exists?
rows.value: Free Rent Board counseling (not legal advice), tenant counselors, eviction-court free legal help, Tenant Right to Counsel for eviction proceedings, and tenant petitions before an ALJ.
rows.notes: No official general rent-increase attorney approval service found.

rows.label: Can increases pass a SF tenant lawyer's review as reasonable, normal business practice, nondiscriminatory and lawful?
rows.notes: No official source can certify approval; only a conservative checklist capable of review.

rows.label: Should one unit or both be raised to avoid discrimination lawsuits/inquiries?
rows.notes: No official rule requires both; use identical neutral criteria and document eligibility reasons if only one is raised.

rows.label: Is a market-rate reset available after Unit 1's roommate change?
rows.notes: Continuing occupant legal status and last-original-occupant facts unverified; no reset recommended.

rows.label: Do individual owners (not corporations) need to apply for the Rent Board license and inform the Rent Board before notifying tenants?
rows.value: Yes for covered annual/banked increases: report into the Housing Inventory and have a current license before the effective date. No individual-owner exemption was found. The pages do not expressly require a separate Board filing before mailing an ordinary notice.
rows.notes: Safest sequence is report/verify license before serving notice; petition-based increases have separate pre-notice filing rules.

rows.label: Is there a separate form to tell the Rent Board about each individual increase?
rows.value: No separate pre-notice Board filing requirement was found for ordinary annual/banked increases; the license arises from Housing Inventory reporting. Petition/worksheet-based increases differ.
rows.notes: Absence of a stated requirement, not an official confirmation; confirm with a counselor.

rows.label: What happens if a notice goes out without a current license?
rows.value: The increase may be null and void, the tenant may be entitled to a refund and may petition the Rent Board, which can schedule an Administrative Law Judge hearing.
rows.notes: A tenant summary petition also prompts a letter to the landlord.

rows.label: Does the added roommate allow a market-rate reset?
rows.value: Not by itself. Extra rent for an added occupant is unlawful. A 6.14 increase requires last-original-occupant vacancy plus timely 6.14 notice; Costa-Hawkins has different subtenant/assignee conditions and does not require a 6.14 notice.
rows.notes: Continuing occupant status and residency facts are unverified; no reset recommended.

rows.label: Is the Rent Board Fee the same thing as the Rent Increase License?
rows.value: No. They are separate obligations. The license comes from Housing Inventory reporting and there is no charge for that reporting; the fee is a separate per-unit annual payment (2026-2027: $59.00 per dwelling unit, due March 1, with a 5% monthly late penalty to a 15% maximum). SF.gov states expressly that requesting a fee exemption does not satisfy Housing Inventory reporting.
rows.notes: Paying the fee is not a substitute for the license; see flag F33.

rows.label: Can part of the Rent Board Fee be charged to the tenants?
rows.value: Yes, if the fee is paid in full: 50% of the fee, i.e. $29.50 per dwelling unit for 2026-2027, may be recovered from tenants in occupancy as of November 1 of the applicable tax year. Penalties may not be recovered.
rows.notes: This is a fee recovery, not a rent increase; keep it separately identified.

rows.label: How long do I have to report a Housing Inventory change, and what if I already served a notice?
rows.value: Report and verify the license, then obtain legal advice on any already-served notice; do not backdate or assume a later license retroactively cures it.
rows.notes: Unit information updates annually by March 1; owner/manager contact changes within 30 days.

rows.label: Can an increase during a repair dispute or after a complaint be retaliatory?
rows.value: It can be. Civil Code 1942.5 has conditional 180-day provisions and broader protection against retaliation for organizing or lawful rights; good-faith cause and other statutory conditions require fact review.
rows.notes: No timing or repair/complaint history was supplied; this is not a legal opinion.

rows.label: Are these two units exempt from AB 1482 because the owner lives in one?
rows.value: Only if the owner occupied one unit as a principal residence when the tenancy began and continues in occupancy, and neither unit is an ADU/JADU. That fact was not supplied, so no exemption is asserted. Independently, AB 1482's rent cap does not apply where the unit is already under the SF Rent Ordinance limits, which are stricter.
rows.notes: Conditional; see flags F34 and F35.

rows.label: Does an in-law unit or a second structure change whether these units are covered?
rows.value: It can. SF.gov states that a single-family dwelling with a legal in-law unit is a two-unit building and is not exempt, that with an illegal in-law unit it is also a two-unit building and is not exempt unless both units are rented together as a single tenancy, and that a single-family dwelling is not exempt if another residential structure is on the same lot. Two rented units is consistent with Rent Ordinance coverage, but the official lot and building record was not supplied.
rows.notes: Verify the lot in the Property Information Map; see flags F35 and F36.

rows.label: Do the tenants have to keep accepting increases, or can they challenge each one?
rows.value: They can challenge. A tenant may file an unlawful-rent-increase petition with no filing fee and no time limit, and the matter can go to an Administrative Law Judge. Tenant-side free legal help is documented for eviction proceedings (Eviction Defense Collaborative line and Tenant Right to Counsel), not as a general pre-approval service for rent increases.
rows.notes: No official source offers approval of an increase before it is served.

rows.label: Is any increase guaranteed lawful or lawsuit-proof?
rows.value: No. No attorney approval or guarantee of no complaint/inquiry/lawsuit is claimed.
rows.notes: Conservative compliance checklist only.

rows.label: Can rent be raised during a fixed-term lease?
rows.value: Generally no, unless the rental agreement expressly allows rent increases; periodic tenancies use statutory notice rules.
rows.notes: Actual lease type/clause unverified; no mid-term increase approved.

rows.label: Does an individual two-unit owner need City business registration?
rows.value: Only rental income from one residential structure with fewer than four units generally does not by itself require registration; other business activity/payroll may require it.
rows.notes: Structure/lot and other activity unverified; no case exemption asserted.

rows.label: Does anonymizing the current site erase earlier public exposure?
rows.value: No. Current placeholders do not rewrite public history, PR diffs, clones or caches; the exposure is disclosed and owner remediation options are listed.
rows.notes: No raw identifiers are reproduced; see F26/F38.

Fact-specific, not an automatic bar for every repair request.
rows.notes: State · checked 2026-11-08

rows.label: California Civil Code — CIV 1947.12 (AB 1482) - two-unit exemption text
rows.value: The state rent cap does not apply to a property with two separate dwelling units in a single structure where the owner occupied one unit as the principal residence at the beginning of the tenancy and continues in occupancy, and neither unit is an ADU or JADU. Exemption for separately alienable property requires the owner notice and that the owner is not a REIT, corporation, or an LLC with at least one corporate member. Verified from the statute text 2026-11-07.
rows.notes: State · checked 2026-11-08

rows.label: SF Rent Board — Partial Exemption for Newly Constructed Rental Units
rows.value: Units whose first Certificate of Occupancy issued after June 13, 1979 are exempt from the rent increase limitations only; they keep just-cause eviction protection and the annual Rent Board fee is collected for them. The exemption needs both a post-June-13-1979 first Certificate of Occupancy and no residential use before it. Re-verified 2026-11-07.
rows.notes: Local · checked 2026-11-08

rows.label: SF Rent Board — Partial Exemption for Certain Single-Family Homes and Condominiums Under Costa-Hawkins
rows.value: As of January 1, 1999, single-family homes and condominiums are generally exempt from the rent increase limitations (but not just cause) only if the tenancy commenced on or after January 1, 1996; a tenancy that commenced before that date stays fully covered. A single-family dwelling with a LEGAL in-law unit constitutes a two-unit building and is not exempt. A single-family dwelling with an ILLEGAL in-law unit also constitutes a two-unit building and is not exempt UNLESS both units are rented together as a single tenancy. A single-family dwelling is not exempt if another residential structure is on the same lot. Exempt units still owe the annual Rent Board fee. Wording corrected 2026-11-08 after line-by-line comparison with the page (see flag F36).
rows.notes: Local · checked 2026-11-08

rows.label: SF Rent Board — Evictions in San Francisco
rows.value: Eviction requires just cause under the Rent Ordinance; the Rent Ordinance generally allows tenants to replace departing roommates and to increase the number of occupants even when a written lease prohibits it; free legal help through the Eviction Defense Collaborative (415-659-9184) on receipt of an unlawful detainer; the 17 just-cause reasons are listed separately. Re-verified 2026-11-07.
rows.notes: Local · checked 2026-11-08

rows.label: SF Rent Board — Recover part of your Rent Board fee from the tenant
rows.value: A landlord who has paid the Rent Board fee in full may collect 50% (excluding late penalties) from the tenant(s) residing in the unit, and only if the tenant resided there on or before November 1 of the year before the fee became due. Recovery is by deducting the amount from the annual security-deposit interest payment, or by billing directly only where there is no or insufficient deposit held or the landlord already pays interest annually. The bill must state the fee amount for each year, any deposit interest owed, that the purpose is to fund the Rent Board, and that the fee is due within 30 days. Unrecovered fees may be banked. A tenant's failure to pay is not a just cause for eviction; collection is through Small Claims Court. Re-verified 2026-11-08.
rows.notes: Local · checked 2026-11-08

rows.label: SF Admin Code — Chapter 37A Rent Stabilization and Arbitration Fee (official PDF)
rows.value: Sec. 37A.1 makes the chapter apply to all residential units, including units exempt from the Chapter 37 rent-increase limits under Costa-Hawkins or Sec. 37.3(d). Sec. 37A.4: fees are due March 1, with 5% added if unpaid by March 1, a further 5% if unpaid by April 1, and a further 5% if unpaid by May 1; referrals to the Bureau of Delinquent Revenue after June 1. Sec. 37A.6: recovery limited to 50% of the annual fee, exclusive of penalties, from tenants in occupancy on November 1, by deposit-interest deduction or a compliant direct bill, may be banked for fees due after July 25, 1999, and the owner remains liable for the full fee whether or not recovery is sought. Re-verified 2026-11-08.
rows.notes: Local · checked 2026-11-08

rows.label: SF Rent Board — Form 573 Rent Board Fee History 25-26 (official PDF)
rows.value: Fee history table: $59.00 per unit and $29.50 tenant share for each tax year 7/21-6/22 through 7/25-6/26 (the newest row). Earlier rows are $50.00 (7/19-6/21), $45.00, $40.00, $37.00, $36.00, $29.00, $26.00, $22.00, $20.00, $27.00, $19.00 and $16.00. States that owners pay per dwelling unit unless a current exemption is approved, that recovery is 50% by deducting from security-deposit interest, and that the tenant must have been in occupancy on November 1 of the tax year. Title says 25-26 and has no 2026-2027 row (see flag F40). Re-verified 2026-11-08.
rows.notes: Local · checked 2026-11-08

rows.label: SF Rent Board — Notification of Rent Board Fee and Housing Inventory Requirements (2027 Informational Notice)
rows.value: 2027 informational notice: no payment is required at this time; the assessment is the basis for the Annual Fee Notice mailed in January 2027; vacant units are subject to the fee and do not qualify for an exemption; an exemption request must be submitted every year by Monday, December 14, 2026; requesting a fee exemption does not satisfy Housing Inventory reporting; Housing Inventory reporting is due March 1, 2027 and annually; landlords will not receive a rent increase license until reporting is complete; occupants of unreported units may receive a noncompliance notice; some increases given without a license will be null and void. Re-verified 2026-11-08.
rows.notes: Local · checked 2026-11-08

rows.label: SF Treasurer & Tax Collector — Information for Lessors of Residential Real Estate
rows.value: A person receiving rental income from one residential structure consisting of fewer than four units (or one residential condominium) is not, by reason of that fact alone, required to obtain a business registration certificate; other business activity or payroll may require one. For the Gross Receipts Tax and Business Registration Fee a lessor is treated as a separate person for each individual building, and the Tax Collector decides what constitutes a separate building and the number of units. A lessor must file a return unless leasing fewer than 4 units in any individual building, and is exempt from the Gross Receipts Tax if leasing fewer than 4 units in any individual building. Re-verified 2026-11-08.
rows.notes: Local · checked 2026-11-08

rows.label: SF Rent Board — Security Deposits (interest rate and AB 12 deposit cap)
rows.value: The security-deposit interest rate for March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 4.2%; interest is owed annually on the tenant's annual due date for deposits held over one year and may not be compounded. AB 12 caps a dwelling-unit deposit at one month's rent for deposits collected on or after July 1, 2024, with an exception allowing two months' rent where the owner is a natural person (or an LLC whose members are all natural persons) and owns no more than 2 residential rental properties totalling no more than 4 dwelling units offered for rent. Re-verified 2026-11-08.
